guides.title: Missing jumps? Separate aim errors from early and late taps
guides.description: Diagnose overshoots, undershoots and aim-tap coordination, then choose a focused practice exercise.

sections.title: Start with three misses, not your worst miss
sections.body: Choose three recent attempts on one difficulty with identical mods and rate. Review a few objects before each miss at reduced playback speed. Record the object time, cursor position at the input and whether the cursor entered the target before or after that input. A miss alone cannot tell you whether spacing, timing or reading caused the error. If the replay cannot resolve the input clearly, mark it uncertain rather than prescribing an aim fix.

sections.title: Find the mistake you actually repeat
sections.body: If the cursor is short of the target at the tap and reaches it afterwards, compare early tapping with incomplete movement. If it travels beyond the target, inspect whether the tap happened during the crossing or after leaving. If the cursor reaches the target but departs before the tap, work on coordination rather than simply moving faster. These are observations about cursor and input order; they do not establish what your eyes or hands intended.

sections.title: Practice: controlled arrivals
sections.body: Suggested drill: choose a short jump section whose rhythm you can already tap comfortably. Play three attempts, concentrating on arriving at each target in time for the tap rather than rushing toward the next object. Reduce rate or spacing if nearly every jump breaks down, but change only one demand. Review the same misses afterwards. Count cursor-outside-at-input events as well as misses: a lucky pass is not the same as repeatable control.

sections.title: Check transfer before increasing difficulty
sections.body: Replay the original section at its original settings, then try a second map with comparable spacing and rhythm. Compare several attempts rather than only the best one. If the practised section improves but the second map does not, keep the drill but add more pattern variety. If inputs remain early despite more controlled arrivals, switch your next practice focus to timing instead of continuing to increase spacing.

sections.title: Watch and apply
sections.body: Tonehh's aim guide is an optional companion video. After watching, choose one idea to test against your own replay evidence. The exercises here are AimMod practice suggestions, not a transcript of the video or a guarantee that one aiming style works for everyone.

sources.title: Watch: Tonehh - osu! How to ACTUALLY improve your aim, Part 1

guides.title: Streams and bursts: find where your tapping breaks down
guides.description: Separate starting a burst, maintaining rhythm and aiming a stream before increasing speed or length.

sections.title: Compare the beginning and end of the pattern
sections.body: Review several bursts at the same rate. Does the first tap miss, does accuracy drift through the middle, or do extra taps continue after the pattern ends? Also check whether the cursor remains on the objects. A late first input followed by steady spacing is a different problem from inputs that progressively fall behind. Do not label every stream miss as insufficient speed.

sections.title: Use note spacing, not BPM alone
sections.body: BPM describes the musical tempo, not how many notes you must tap each second. Note subdivision matters: a quarter-beat stream and a half-beat pattern at the same BPM require different tapping rates. Compare subdivision, burst length, spacing and rate-changing mods together. Start with patterns you can distinguish visually and rhythmically before using them to assess sustained tapping.

sections.title: Practice: change length before speed
sections.body: Suggested drill: select short bursts at a comfortable fixed rate. Play a few attempts with attention to starting and stopping at the intended notes. Then compare slightly longer bursts at the same rate. If short bursts are consistent but longer ones deteriorate, work on maintaining the rhythm over length. If both fail at their first note, review the transition into the burst before increasing duration. Keep breaks between sets; stop a session rather than trying to push through discomfort.

sections.title: Keep a useful result log
sections.body: Record the map difficulty, rate, approximate burst length, accuracy and where the first error occurred. Compare a handful of fresh attempts on another day, not just repetitions immediately after memorising the section. Success means the same demand is more consistent across different patterns. A single high-speed pass or an improvement on only one memorised stream is not enough to establish that.

sources.title: Watch: osu! phd: a comprehensive introduction to every skill

guides.title: Turn your replay mistakes into a useful practice session
guides.description: Choose one recurring weakness, practise it in context and check improvement without chasing only your best score.

sections.title: Choose one question for today
sections.body: Use recent plays that reflect your current ability. Pick a recurring observation across multiple attempts: leaving circles before tapping, losing rhythm after a burst, or breaking down when a pattern becomes denser. Write a testable question such as: can I keep inputs on target through this transition? Avoid goals like improve everything or gain a fixed amount of PP in one session.

sections.title: Establish a baseline
sections.body: Choose two or three relevant maps and keep their difficulty, client, mods and rate fixed. Record a few attempts including failures. Note section misses and accuracy, not only the final score. Different patterns with similar stars are not interchangeable, so choose maps that actually contain the demand you want to test.

sections.title: Repeat the section with its lead-in
sections.body: Suggested drill: practise the difficult section with enough preceding objects to preserve the transition and rhythm. Use a short group of repetitions with breaks rather than immediately retrying indefinitely. Change one variable, such as rate, only when you cannot complete enough of the pattern to learn from it. Do not remove every lead-in object: hitting an isolated pattern is not the same task as entering it during a full play.

sections.title: Finish with a transfer check
sections.body: Return to the original settings for a complete attempt, then test a different map with the same demand. Compare the repeated error and the judgement breakdown with your baseline. Keep the exercise if both show improvement across attempts. If only the rehearsed section improves, add variation next time. If the error changes, update your practice question rather than repeating an exercise just because it once helped.

sections.title: Review the week, not only the personal best
sections.body: Compare recent sessions using the same settings and retain unsuccessful attempts. Look for fewer repeated errors and more consistent results before raising the challenge. Keep score targets separate from practice targets: one seeks a strong result with existing skills; the other deliberately exposes a weakness. Use PP as one result measure, not the only definition of a productive session.

sources.title: Watch: osu! phd: a comprehensive introduction to every skill

guides.title: osu! PP and star rating: what each number means
guides.description: Separate map difficulty, score PP and weighted profile PP when choosing your next osu! practice target.

sections.title: Difficulty is not a predicted result
sections.body: Star rating describes calculated beatmap difficulty. Performance points evaluate a score using the map and the performance achieved on it. A star rating alone does not say whether you can play the map accurately. Two maps with similar stars can ask for different combinations of cursor movement, tapping and reading.

sections.title: A score's PP is not its profile gain
sections.body: Profile PP weights scores according to their position among your best performances. A new 200 PP score does not necessarily add 200 PP to your profile. Difficulty and performance calculations can also change after official updates; compare estimates made with the same calculator version and mod settings.

sections.title: Review exercise
sections.body: Choose two maps near your comfortable star range. Compare note rate, spacing and the sections where you lose accuracy, then play both with the same mods. Keep the better-matched map as a score target and the other as a specific practice task. Treat an SS calculation as a scenario, not a promise of the result you will achieve.

guides.title: Review osu! replay mistakes without guessing the cause
guides.description: Check cursor position, tap timing and slider events before turning an osu! replay miss into a practice decision.

sections.title: Start with the event
sections.body: A replay lets you revisit a play rather than relying on memory. For a missed circle, inspect where the cursor was when the tap happened and whether the tap was inside the judgement window. A cursor passing through the circle at some other time is not enough to establish a successful hit.

sections.title: Separate slider parts
sections.body: A slider has a head and additional events along its path. A failed slider event is not automatically a missed head. Compare the relevant event and scoring rules before counting it as an aim or timing mistake. An analysis label such as overshoot or late click is a hypothesis about that event, not a complete explanation of your technique.

sections.title: Review exercise
sections.body: Pick three mistakes, including one from a failed attempt. Watch the lead-in, the input and the next object. Write one observation for each: cursor outside on tap, no observed tap, or late input, for example. When the evidence is ambiguous, leave the cause unknown. Compare several similar sections before choosing a practice focus.

guides.title: Choose osu! pattern practice by spacing and rhythm
guides.description: Compare jumps, bursts and streams using spacing, note intervals and repeated replay evidence instead of stars alone.

sections.title: Name the demand, not just the map
sections.body: Streams are sequences of closely timed objects. Within a sequence, spacing and direction can still vary. A short fast burst and a long stream need not expose the same difficulty for you. For practice selection, record the duration of the difficult section as well as how quickly notes arrive and how far the cursor must travel.

sections.title: Compare like with like
sections.body: Keep the ruleset and rate settings fixed when comparing attempts. A comfortable jump map is not proof that you can maintain accuracy on a dense stream at the same star rating. Look for repeated success and repeated misses on similar sections across different maps, rather than treating your best play as your typical result.

sections.title: Review exercise
sections.body: Select a small group of maps with a shared pattern demand. Play a baseline attempt, choose one observable problem and review another attempt after practice. Change one demand at a time: spacing, note rate or section length. Keep failed attempts in the comparison. This is a way to structure your review, not a guarantee of a particular improvement rate.

guides.title: Compare osu! stable, lazer and Classic scores fairly
guides.description: Keep client, slider judgement and mod settings in view when comparing osu! stable and lazer performance.

sections.title: Record the rules used
sections.body: Stable and lazer are not interchangeable labels for an identical scoring environment. The official migration guide documents gameplay differences, including slider behaviour, grading and input handling. Classic can restore selected legacy behaviours; it is not a reason to assume every setting or result is identical to stable.

sections.title: Use matched comparisons
sections.body: When accuracy changes after switching clients, first check the beatmap version, mods and their settings. Compare the judgement breakdown and slider-head results before concluding that your timing has become worse. Keep each score's original client and ruleset context with your notes.

sections.title: Review exercise
sections.body: Choose a familiar map and record the settings for each play. Review circles and slider heads separately where the available analysis supports that distinction. Do not average unlike score totals into a single improvement claim. Consult the official upgrading guide for current compatibility and migration details rather than relying on an old feature checklist.

sources.title: osu! help centre: Upgrading to lazer

guides.title: Keep osu! mods and rate settings in your practice notes
guides.description: Understand why mod acronyms alone are not enough to compare osu! practice attempts and difficulty estimates.

sections.title: Mods change the task
sections.body: Game modifiers can alter beatmap settings and gameplay. A rate-changing setup changes the time available between objects; visibility or difficulty settings can change a different part of the task. Do not treat an identical beatmap title as evidence that two attempts presented identical demands.

sections.title: Save settings, not only acronyms
sections.body: Lazer supports settings within mods. When a custom setting is used, keep its value alongside the acronym. Compare difficulty and performance estimates under the same effective setup, and check the client for the current scoring eligibility of that combination. An estimate is not confirmation that a score will be submitted or ranked.

sections.title: Review exercise
sections.body: Start with your usual setup and change one setting. Note the exact rate, then compare the same section for accuracy and miss location. Keep the original attempt as the baseline. If a slower attempt becomes cleaner, test again at the original rate before concluding that the practice transfers to your score target.

guides.title: Read osu! accuracy, combo and score together
guides.description: Use judgement counts and scoring context to compare osu! attempts without confusing score, accuracy, combo and PP.

sections.title: Each number answers a different question
sections.body: Accuracy summarizes judgement quality. Combo records a consecutive sequence, while total score follows the scoring system in use. PP is a separate performance calculation. A larger score total alone is not enough to conclude that every part of the play improved.

sections.title: Check the breakdown
sections.body: Compare the counts of 300s, 100s, 50s and misses, then inspect where those results occurred. Keep slider events and the client context in mind. A whole-play percentage can conceal a short difficult section, and a failed attempt may only contain evidence for the portion that was played.

sections.title: Review exercise
sections.body: Place two attempts on the same map and setup side by side. Record accuracy, miss count, maximum combo and whether the play reached the end. Identify one section that improved and one that still breaks down. Keep unknown completion or missing analysis explicitly unknown instead of filling the gap with a favourable assumption.
